reading.passage: A big lion is sleeping. A little mouse runs over his face. The lion wakes up and catches the mouse. 'Please let me go,' says the mouse. 'One day I can help you.' The lion laughs, but he lets the mouse go. Two days later, the mouse sees the lion in a net. He bites the net with his small teeth, and the lion is free.
reading.q: What is the lion doing at the start of the story?
reading.answer: Sleeping

reading.passage: A big lion is sleeping. A little mouse runs over his face. The lion wakes up and catches the mouse. 'Please let me go,' says the mouse. 'One day I can help you.' The lion laughs, but he lets the mouse go. Two days later, the mouse sees the lion in a net. He bites the net with his small teeth, and the lion is free.
reading.q: Why does the lion laugh?
options: The mouse tells a funny story.
He thinks a mouse cannot help him.
He wants to eat the mouse.
reading.answer: He thinks a mouse cannot help him.

reading.passage: A big lion is sleeping. A little mouse runs over his face. The lion wakes up and catches the mouse. 'Please let me go,' says the mouse. 'One day I can help you.' The lion laughs, but he lets the mouse go. Two days later, the mouse sees the lion in a net. He bites the net with his small teeth, and the lion is free.
reading.q: In the story, 'free' means ___.
reading.answer: out of the net

reading.passage: A big lion is sleeping. A little mouse runs over his face. The lion wakes up and catches the mouse. 'Please let me go,' says the mouse. 'One day I can help you.' reading.q: What is the best title for the story?
reading.answer: The Lion and the Mouse

reading.passage: It is summer. A grasshopper sings and plays all day. An ant works hard and puts food in her house. 'Come and play with me,' says the grasshopper. 'No, I am busy,' says the ant. 'Winter is coming.' Cold winter comes. The grasshopper has no food and no house. He goes to the ant's house. 'Please give me some food,' he says. The ant gives him bread, but she says, 'Work and play at the right time.'
reading.q: What does the ant do in summer?
reading.answer: She works and saves food.

reading.answer: He needs food.

reading.passage: A crow is very thirsty. He looks for water. He finds a tall jar. There is a little water in it. The crow cannot reach the water. He has an idea. He drops small stones into the jar. The water comes up. The crow drinks and is happy.
reading.q: What does the crow want?
reading.answer: Water

reading.q: Why does the crow drop stones into the jar?
options: To make the water come up
reading.answer: To make the water come up

reading.q: In the story, 'an idea' means ___.
options: a thought or plan in the head
reading.answer: a thought or plan in the head

reading.passage: A crow is very thirsty. He looks for water. He finds a tall jar. There is a little water in it. The crow cannot reach the water. He has an idea. He drops small stones into the jar. The water comes up. The crow drinks and is happy.
reading.q: What is the story mainly about?
reading.answer: A clever bird getting water

reading.passage: A little red hen finds some seeds. She wants to make bread. She asks the dog, the cat and the duck for help. They all say no. The hen plants the seeds and waters them. She makes the bread alone. 'Who will help me eat it?' she asks. 'We will!' say the dog, the cat and the duck. 'No,' says the hen. 'I will eat it with my chicks.'
reading.q: What does the little red hen want to make?
reading.answer: Bread

reading.passage: A little red hen finds some seeds. She wants to make bread. She asks the dog, the cat and the duck for help. They all say no. The hen plants the seeds and waters them. She makes the bread alone. 'Who will help me eat it?' she asks. 'We will!' say the dog, the cat and the duck. 'No,' says the hen. 'I will eat it with my chicks.'
reading.q: Why does the hen not share the bread?
options: The animals did not help her.
reading.answer: The animals did not help her.

reading.q: In the story, 'alone' means ___.
reading.answer: with no one else helping

reading.passage: A little red hen finds some seeds. She wants to make bread. She asks the dog, the cat and the duck for help. They all say no. The hen plants the seeds and waters them. She makes the bread alone. 'Who will help me eat it?' she asks. 'We will!' say the dog, the cat and the duck. 'No,' says the hen. 'I will eat it with my chicks.'
reading.q: What is the story mainly about?
options: A dog and a cat who like bread
A hen who works by herself and then eats by herself
A hen who makes bread for everyone
reading.answer: A hen who works by herself and then eats by herself

reading.passage: A hare laughs at a tortoise. 'You are so slow!' he says. The tortoise says, 'Let us have a race.' The race starts. The hare runs very fast. Soon he is far ahead. He thinks, 'I have time. I will take a nap.' The tortoise keeps walking slowly. He does not stop. When the hare wakes up, the tortoise is near the finish line. The tortoise wins the race.
reading.q: What does the hare do during the race?
reading.answer: He takes a nap.

reading.q: Why does the tortoise win the race?
options: He keeps walking and never stops.
He runs faster than the hare.
The hare cannot find the way.
reading.answer: He keeps walking and never stops.

reading.q: In the story, 'a nap' means ___.
reading.answer: a short sleep

options: Keep trying, even if you are slow.
reading.answer: Keep trying, even if you are slow.

reading.passage: A shepherd boy looks after sheep on a hill. He is bored. He shouts, 'Wolf! Wolf! A wolf is here!' The villagers run up the hill with sticks. But there is no wolf. The boy laughs. The next day he does it again. The villagers are angry. On the third day, a real wolf comes. The boy shouts for help, but nobody comes. The wolf eats the sheep.
reading.q: What is the boy's job?
reading.answer: To look after sheep

reading.passage: A shepherd boy looks after sheep on a hill. He is bored. He shouts, 'Wolf! Wolf! A wolf is here!' The villagers run up the hill with sticks. But there is no wolf. The boy laughs. reading.q: Why do the villagers not come on the third day?
options: They do not believe the boy.
They are afraid of the wolf.

reading.passage:
A community garden is a piece of land that local people use to grow vegetables, fruit and flowers. Some gardens are on empty land beside a road. Others are on the roof of a building. People who live nearby can rent a small part of the garden and grow their own food.

These gardens are popular in many cities. They give people a chance to spend time outside and to meet their neighbours. Children can learn where food comes from. Some gardens also give part of their vegetables to food banks, which give free food to people who need it.

A community garden needs hard work. Someone must collect the rent, buy tools and plan the work for the year. In most gardens, the members do this together, and they meet once a month to talk about problems. The meetings are important, because a garden only works when everyone helps.
reading.q: Who can rent a small part of a community garden?
reading.answer: People who live nearby

Bees do much more than make honey. They also move pollen from one flower to another, and this helps plants make fruit and seeds. Scientists say that a large part of the food we grow depends on the work of bees and other insects.

For a long time, people thought that bees could only be kept in the countryside. Now more and more people keep bees on the roofs of buildings in the city. Bees can find flowers in parks and gardens, and city flowers often have fewer harmful chemicals than farm flowers. City bees may even make more honey than country bees.

Beekeeping is not always easy. A person who wants to keep bees must learn how to look after them, and some people are afraid of bees. For this reason, beekeepers often talk to their neighbours before they put a hive on the roof.

reading.answer: They move pollen between flowers

reading.passage:
Plastic is cheap and strong, and it has changed the way we live. Bags, bottles and food packages are made of it, and most of these things are used only once. When people throw them away, they often end up in rivers and oceans.

Plastic does not rot like food or paper. Sunlight breaks it into very small pieces, but these pieces stay in the water for many years. Fish and sea birds sometimes eat them by mistake, and some animals get caught in larger pieces of plastic. The plastic can also travel long distances, so a bottle dropped in one country may reach a beach in another.

Governments and companies have started to act. Some cities have stopped shops from giving free plastic bags, and some companies now sell drinks in bottles that can be returned and reused. These changes help, but experts say that the most important step is to make less plastic in the first place.

Many people think of a museum as a quiet building full of old objects behind glass. In fact, the best museums are busy places of learning. Visitors can touch copies of ancient tools, listen to stories from people who lived through history, or take part in experiments in a science room. These activities help people understand ideas that a label on a wall can never explain.

Researchers who study how people learn in museums have found something surprising. Visitors usually forget most of the facts they read. They do remember objects that made them feel something, such as a heavy sword, a beautifully painted bowl, or a machine that suddenly worked. Such memories can last for years.

For teachers, this means that a museum visit should not be a race through every room. It is better to spend time on a few objects and to ask questions than to see everything quickly. What students bring home is not a list of dates, but a picture in their minds of how people lived and thought.

Read every label in silence alone
Buy old objects to take home
reading.answer: Touch copies of ancient tools and join activities

Public transport is any system that carries many people at once: buses, trains, trams and underground railways. A single bus can hold more than fifty passengers, which means that one bus can replace dozens of cars on a busy road. For this reason, cities that invest in good public transport often have less traffic and cleaner air.

However, good public transport is expensive. Trains must be built and repaired, and staff must be paid. Fares cover only part of the cost, so the rest must come from taxes. This is why some people ask whether it is fair for everyone to pay for a service that only some people use.

Supporters answer that public transport helps everyone, even those who never travel on it. If buses and trains take cars off the road, drivers save time, and hospitals spend less money on illnesses caused by dirty air. Seen in this way, public transport is not simply a service for passengers; it is an investment in the whole city.
reading.q: What happens in cities that invest in good public transport?
options: There is less traffic and cleaner air
reading.answer: There is less traffic and cleaner air

For most of history, the sky was something people could only look at. That changed in the twentieth century. In 1957, a small satellite called Sputnik became the first human-made object to orbit the Earth, and only twelve years later people walked on the Moon. Since then, spacecraft have visited every planet in our solar system, and telescopes in space have looked back towards the beginning of the universe.

Space travel is extremely expensive, and some people argue that the money would be better spent on problems closer to home, such as health care and clean water. Others point out that space research has given us everyday technologies, from better water filters to satellite navigation. They also argue that studying other planets helps us understand the climate of our own.

Perhaps the strongest argument for space exploration is less practical. Looking at the Earth from far away changes the way people think about it. Many astronauts have described seeing the planet as a small, fragile ball. This experience has led some of them to work for peace and for the protection of the environment.

options: The first human-made satellite began to orbit the Earth
reading.answer: The first human-made satellite began to orbit the Earth

Every new technology changes the kind of work people do, and artificial intelligence is no different. Computers can already write simple reports, answer customers' questions and sort huge amounts of data, work that used to take people many hours. Some jobs will certainly disappear, especially those that involve repeating the same steps again and again.

History suggests, however, that such changes rarely happen as quickly as people fear. When machines took over farm work, millions of people moved into factories; later, when factories became more efficient, many workers found jobs in offices and shops. Each change caused real hardship for some families, but the number of jobs did not simply fall to zero.

The more useful question may be not how many jobs will remain, but which skills will be valued. Tasks that require judgement, creativity and the ability to work with other people are harder for machines to copy. Education systems that teach facts alone may therefore prepare students badly. Those that encourage curiosity, communication and problem-solving are more likely to help young people in a world where the tools they use are changing all the time.

options: Jobs that involve repeating the same steps
Jobs that involve working with people
reading.answer: Jobs that involve repeating the same steps

Many teenagers go to bed with their phones and wake up with them as well. At first, this seems harmless: a few messages, a video or two, and then sleep. In fact, researchers who study sleep have found that using a phone late at night can make it harder to fall asleep and can make sleep shorter. The light from a screen tells the brain that it is still daytime, and exciting content keeps the mind busy.

There is also a social side to the problem. Messages arrive all night, and young people often feel that they must answer quickly, even when they are tired. This can turn rest into another kind of work. Many teenagers say that they would like to use their phones less at night but do not want to be the first in their group to stop.

Some schools and families are trying simple solutions. They charge phones in the kitchen, set a time after which the phone stays downstairs, or agree that group chats go quiet at night. The aim is not to win a battle against technology, but to protect a few hours in which the mind can rest.
reading.q: What does the light from a screen do, according to researchers?
options: It tells the brain that it is still daytime
It makes the phone battery hot
reading.answer: It tells the brain that it is still daytime

Anyone who has tried to learn a foreign language knows the strange gap between understanding a rule and being able to use it. A student can explain perfectly when to use the past tense and still say the wrong form in a conversation. Teachers have argued for decades about the reason for this gap and about what should be done in the classroom.

One group believes that grammar should be taught directly, step by step, so that learners build a clear system that they can rely on later. Another group argues that learners acquire language best when they meet many understandable messages, much as children do, and that grammar lessons are of limited value. Many researchers now take a position between these extremes: some focused attention on form helps, but only when it is connected to real use.

What seems beyond doubt is the importance of time and practice. Learners who read and listen widely, and who are not afraid of making mistakes, generally make faster progress than those who wait until they know every rule. In other words, confidence matters as much as knowledge, and it is built by using the language, not by studying it forever.
reading.q: What is the “strange gap” described at the beginning of the passage?
options: The time it takes to learn a language
The difference between knowing a rule and using it correctly
reading.answer: The difference between knowing a rule and using it correctly

reading.passage:
Social media platforms are designed to keep people looking. Their engineers have learned that a new message, a “like” or a short video gives the brain a small reward, and that unclear or upsetting content often holds attention longer than calm and sensible material. The result is a system that is extremely good at what it was built to do, and it is exactly this success that worries critics.

Some of the concern is easy to understand: spending hours online takes time away from sleep, exercise and face-to-face conversation. But a more subtle worry is that the platforms shape what people believe without them noticing. If a person sees mostly posts that agree with their opinions, they may gradually become more certain that everyone thinks as they do, and less willing to consider other views.

Defenders of social media reply that the same tools allow people to organise, learn and find others like themselves. Rather than blaming the technology, they argue that we should teach people to use it deliberately. That means choosing what they follow, noticing when they are being pulled into an argument, and deciding when to put the phone down. Whether individuals can win such a contest against companies that study human attention for a living remains an open question.
reading.q: What holds attention longer, according to the passage?
options: Short messages that are well written
reading.answer: Unclear or upsetting content

reading.passage:
Social media platforms are designed to keep people looking. Their engineers have learned that a new message, a “like” or a short video gives the brain a small reward, and that unclear or upsetting content often holds attention longer than calm and sensible material. The result is a system that is extremely good at what it was built to do, and it is exactly this success that worries critics.

Some of the concern is easy to understand: spending hours online takes time away from sleep, exercise and face-to-face conversation. But a more subtle worry is that the platforms shape what people believe without them noticing. If a person sees mostly posts that agree with their opinions, they may gradually become more certain that everyone thinks as they do, and less willing to consider other views.

Defenders of social media reply that the same tools allow people to organise, learn and find others like themselves. Rather than blaming the technology, they argue that we should teach people to use it deliberately. That means choosing what they follow, noticing when they are being pulled into an argument, and deciding when to put the phone down. Whether individuals can win such a contest against companies that study human attention for a living remains an open question.
reading.q: What is the writer's position?
options: The platforms have real effects, and it is unclear whether individuals can control them
Social media has no effect on people's beliefs
Everyone should delete their accounts immediately
reading.answer: The platforms have real effects, and it is unclear whether individuals can control them

reading.passage:
Volunteering is work that people do without being paid, usually to help others or to improve the place where they live. It ranges from serving meals in a shelter to teaching a child to read, from planting trees to running a sports club. To an observer, it can look like a gift: time and effort given freely, with nothing expected in return.

The reality is more complicated, because volunteers usually gain as much as they give. Studies of volunteering repeatedly find that regular volunteers report lower levels of loneliness and greater satisfaction with their lives. Some of this may be self-selection — people who are already cheerful may be more likely to volunteer — but the effect appears in experiments too, especially when the work involves meeting people face to face.

There are difficulties as well. Organisations may rely on volunteers to do work that should really be done by paid staff, and volunteers can feel unsupported or unsure whether their effort matters. The most successful organisations treat volunteers as colleagues rather than as free labour, providing clear tasks, training and honest feedback. The difference between a volunteer who returns for years and one who never comes back is often not enthusiasm. It is how useful they were made to feel on the first day.
reading.q: What do studies of volunteering repeatedly find?
options: Volunteers earn less money than other people
Regular volunteers report lower loneliness and greater satisfaction
Volunteers usually become tired and unhappy
reading.answer: Regular volunteers report lower loneliness and greater satisfaction

reading.passage:
The phrase “extreme weather” covers events such as heatwaves, heavy rainfall, droughts and very powerful storms. Such events have always existed, but a growing body of research suggests that a warmer atmosphere changes both their frequency and their strength. Warm air can hold more water, so when rain finally falls it may fall harder; hotter and drier seasons, meanwhile, leave forests and farmland ready to burn.

Attributing any single storm to climate change is difficult, and scientists are usually careful to say that a particular event “was made more likely” rather than that it “was caused” by warming. Nevertheless, statistical work that compares thousands of simulations with and without human influence has become increasingly confident. For some heatwaves, researchers now describe the effect as unmistakable.

The practical question is how cities and farmers should respond. Dams, early-warning systems and trees that shade streets can all reduce damage, and insurance schemes can spread the cost of rebuilding. Yet such measures are expensive, and poorer countries and communities usually have the least money to pay for them. This is one reason why international discussions about climate often turn into arguments about fairness, even when the scientific questions are no longer especially disputed.
reading.q: Why can a warmer atmosphere lead to heavier rain?
options: Because warm air makes clouds darker
Because warm air can hold more water
reading.answer: Because warm air can hold more water

reading.passage:
A community garden is a piece of land that local people use to grow vegetables, fruit and flowers. Some gardens are on empty land beside a road. Others are on the roof of a building. People who live nearby can rent a small part of the garden and grow their own food.

These gardens are popular in many cities. They give people a chance to spend time outside and to meet their neighbours. Children can learn where food comes from. Some gardens also give part of their vegetables to food banks, which give free food to people who need it.

A community garden needs hard work. Someone must collect the rent, buy tools and plan the work for the year. In most gardens, the members do this together, and they meet once a month to talk about problems. The meetings are important, because a garden only works when everyone helps.
reading.q: Who can rent a small part of a community garden?
reading.answer: People who live nearby

Bees do much more than make honey. They also move pollen from one flower to another, and this helps plants make fruit and seeds. Scientists say that a large part of the food we grow depends on the work of bees and other insects.

For a long time, people thought that bees could only be kept in the countryside. Now more and more people keep bees on the roofs of buildings in the city. Bees can find flowers in parks and gardens, and city flowers often have fewer harmful chemicals than farm flowers. City bees may even make more honey than country bees.

Beekeeping is not always easy. A person who wants to keep bees must learn how to look after them, and some people are afraid of bees. For this reason, beekeepers often talk to their neighbours before they put a hive on the roof.

reading.answer: They move pollen between flowers

reading.passage:
Plastic is cheap and strong, and it has changed the way we live. Bags, bottles and food packages are made of it, and most of these things are used only once. When people throw them away, they often end up in rivers and oceans.

Plastic does not rot like food or paper. Sunlight breaks it into very small pieces, but these pieces stay in the water for many years. Fish and sea birds sometimes eat them by mistake, and some animals get caught in larger pieces of plastic. The plastic can also travel long distances, so a bottle dropped in one country may reach a beach in another.

Governments and companies have started to act. Some cities have stopped shops from giving free plastic bags, and some companies now sell drinks in bottles that can be returned and reused. These changes help, but experts say that the most important step is to make less plastic in the first place.

options: It breaks into very small pieces
reading.answer: It breaks into very small pieces

Many people think of a museum as a quiet building full of old objects behind glass. In fact, the best museums are busy places of learning. Visitors can touch copies of ancient tools, listen to stories from people who lived through history, or take part in experiments in a science room. These activities help people understand ideas that a label on a wall can never explain.

Researchers who study how people learn in museums have found something surprising. Visitors usually forget most of the facts they read. They do remember objects that made them feel something, such as a heavy sword, a beautifully painted bowl, or a machine that suddenly worked. Such memories can last for years.

For teachers, this means that a museum visit should not be a race through every room. It is better to spend time on a few objects and to ask questions than to see everything quickly. What students bring home is not a list of dates, but a picture in their minds of how people lived and thought.
reading.q: What can visitors do in the best museums, according to the passage?
options: Touch copies of ancient tools and join activities
Read every label in silence alone
Buy old objects to take home
reading.answer: Touch copies of ancient tools and join activities

Public transport is any system that carries many people at once: buses, trains, trams and underground railways. A single bus can hold more than fifty passengers, which means that one bus can replace dozens of cars on a busy road. For this reason, cities that invest in good public transport often have less traffic and cleaner air.

However, good public transport is expensive. Trains must be built and repaired, and staff must be paid. Fares cover only part of the cost, so the rest must come from taxes. This is why some people ask whether it is fair for everyone to pay for a service that only some people use.

Supporters answer that public transport helps everyone, even those who never travel on it. If buses and trains take cars off the road, drivers save time, and hospitals spend less money on illnesses caused by dirty air. Seen in this way, public transport is not simply a service for passengers; it is an investment in the whole city.
reading.q: What happens in cities that invest in good public transport?
options: There is less traffic and cleaner air
reading.answer: There is less traffic and cleaner air

For most of history, the sky was something people could only look at. That changed in the twentieth century. In 1957, a small satellite called Sputnik became the first human-made object to orbit the Earth, and only twelve years later people walked on the Moon. Since then, spacecraft have visited every planet in our solar system, and telescopes in space have looked back towards the beginning of the universe.

Space travel is extremely expensive, and some people argue that the money would be better spent on problems closer to home, such as health care and clean water. Others point out that space research has given us everyday technologies, from better water filters to satellite navigation. They also argue that studying other planets helps us understand the climate of our own.

Perhaps the strongest argument for space exploration is less practical. Looking at the Earth from far away changes the way people think about it. Many astronauts have described seeing the planet as a small, fragile ball. This experience has led some of them to work for peace and for the protection of the environment.

options: The first human-made satellite began to orbit the Earth
reading.answer: The first human-made satellite began to orbit the Earth

Every new technology changes the kind of work people do, and artificial intelligence is no different. Computers can already write simple reports, answer customers' questions and sort huge amounts of data, work that used to take people many hours. Some jobs will certainly disappear, especially those that involve repeating the same steps again and again.

History suggests, however, that such changes rarely happen as quickly as people fear. When machines took over farm work, millions of people moved into factories; later, when factories became more efficient, many workers found jobs in offices and shops. Each change caused real hardship for some families, but the number of jobs did not simply fall to zero.

The more useful question may be not how many jobs will remain, but which skills will be valued. Tasks that require judgement, creativity and the ability to work with other people are harder for machines to copy. Education systems that teach facts alone may therefore prepare students badly. Those that encourage curiosity, communication and problem-solving are more likely to help young people in a world where the tools they use are changing all the time.
reading.q: According to the passage, which jobs are most likely to disappear?
options: Jobs that involve repeating the same steps
Jobs that involve working with people
reading.answer: Jobs that involve repeating the same steps

Many teenagers go to bed with their phones and wake up with them as well. At first, this seems harmless: a few messages, a video or two, and then sleep. In fact, researchers who study sleep have found that using a phone late at night can make it harder to fall asleep and can make sleep shorter. The light from a screen tells the brain that it is still daytime, and exciting content keeps the mind busy.

There is also a social side to the problem. Messages arrive all night, and young people often feel that they must answer quickly, even when they are tired. This can turn rest into another kind of work. Many teenagers say that they would like to use their phones less at night but do not want to be the first in their group to stop.

Some schools and families are trying simple solutions. They charge phones in the kitchen, set a time after which the phone stays downstairs, or agree that group chats go quiet at night. The aim is not to win a battle against technology, but to protect a few hours in which the mind can rest.
reading.q: What does the light from a screen do, according to researchers?
options: It tells the brain that it is still daytime
It makes the phone battery hot
reading.answer: It tells the brain that it is still daytime

Anyone who has tried to learn a foreign language knows the strange gap between understanding a rule and being able to use it. A student can explain perfectly when to use the past tense and still say the wrong form in a conversation. Teachers have argued for decades about the reason for this gap and about what should be done in the classroom.

One group believes that grammar should be taught directly, step by step, so that learners build a clear system that they can rely on later. Another group argues that learners acquire language best when they meet many understandable messages, much as children do, and that grammar lessons are of limited value. Many researchers now take a position between these extremes: some focused attention on form helps, but only when it is connected to real use.

What seems beyond doubt is the importance of time and practice. Learners who read and listen widely, and who are not afraid of making mistakes, generally make faster progress than those who wait until they know every rule. In other words, confidence matters as much as knowledge, and it is built by using the language, not by studying it forever.
reading.q: What is the “strange gap” described at the beginning of the passage?
options: The time it takes to learn a language
The difference between knowing a rule and using it correctly
reading.answer: The difference between knowing a rule and using it correctly

reading.passage:
Social media platforms are designed to keep people looking. Their engineers have learned that a new message, a “like” or a short video gives the brain a small reward, and that unclear or upsetting content often holds attention longer than calm and sensible material. The result is a system that is extremely good at what it was built to do, and it is exactly this success that worries critics.

Some of the concern is easy to understand: spending hours online takes time away from sleep, exercise and face-to-face conversation. But a more subtle worry is that the platforms shape what people believe without them noticing. If a person sees mostly posts that agree with their opinions, they may gradually become more certain that everyone thinks as they do, and less willing to consider other views.

Defenders of social media reply that the same tools allow people to organise, learn and find others like themselves. Rather than blaming the technology, they argue that we should teach people to use it deliberately. That means choosing what they follow, noticing when they are being pulled into an argument, and deciding when to put the phone down. Whether individuals can win such a contest against companies that study human attention for a living remains an open question.
reading.q: What holds attention longer, according to the passage?
options: Short messages that are well written
reading.answer: Unclear or upsetting content

Volunteering is work that people do without being paid, usually to help others or to improve the place where they live. It ranges from serving meals in a shelter to teaching a child to read, from planting trees to running a sports club. To an observer, it can look like a gift: time and effort given freely, with nothing expected in return.

The reality is more complicated, because volunteers usually gain as much as they give. Studies of volunteering repeatedly find that regular volunteers report lower levels of loneliness and greater satisfaction with their lives. Some of this may be self-selection — people who are already cheerful may be more likely to volunteer — but the effect appears in experiments too, especially when the work involves meeting people face to face.

There are difficulties as well. Organisations may rely on volunteers to do work that should really be done by paid staff, and volunteers can feel unsupported or unsure whether their effort matters. The most successful organisations treat volunteers as colleagues rather than as free labour, providing clear tasks, training and honest feedback. The difference between a volunteer who returns for years and one who never comes back is often not enthusiasm. It is how useful they were made to feel on the first day.
reading.q: What do studies of volunteering repeatedly find?
options: Volunteers earn less money than other people
Regular volunteers report lower loneliness and greater satisfaction
Volunteers usually become tired and unhappy
reading.answer: Regular volunteers report lower loneliness and greater satisfaction

reading.passage:
Volunteering is work that people do without being paid, usually to help others or to improve the place where they live. It ranges from serving meals in a shelter to teaching a child to read, from planting trees to running a sports club. To an observer, it can look like a gift: time and effort given freely, with nothing expected in return.

The reality is more complicated, because volunteers usually gain as much as they give. Studies of volunteering repeatedly find that regular volunteers report lower levels of loneliness and greater satisfaction with their lives. Some of this may be self-selection — people who are already cheerful may be more likely to volunteer — but the effect appears in experiments too, especially when the work involves meeting people face to face.

There are difficulties as well. Organisations may rely on volunteers to do work that should really be done by paid staff, and volunteers can feel unsupported or unsure whether their effort matters. The most successful organisations treat volunteers as colleagues rather than as free labour, providing clear tasks, training and honest feedback. The difference between a volunteer who returns for years and one who never comes back is often not enthusiasm. It is how useful they were made to feel on the first day.
reading.q: Why does the writer mention self-selection?
options: To show that cheerful people are better workers
To argue that volunteering should be paid
To admit that the benefits may partly come from the kind of people who choose to volunteer
reading.answer: To admit that the benefits may partly come from the kind of people who choose to volunteer

reading.passage:
The phrase “extreme weather” covers events such as heatwaves, heavy rainfall, droughts and very powerful storms. Such events have always existed, but a growing body of research suggests that a warmer atmosphere changes both their frequency and their strength. Warm air can hold more water, so when rain finally falls it may fall harder; hotter and drier seasons, meanwhile, leave forests and farmland ready to burn.

Attributing any single storm to climate change is difficult, and scientists are usually careful to say that a particular event “was made more likely” rather than that it “was caused” by warming. Nevertheless, statistical work that compares thousands of simulations with and without human influence has become increasingly confident. For some heatwaves, researchers now describe the effect as unmistakable.

The practical question is how cities and farmers should respond. Dams, early-warning systems and trees that shade streets can all reduce damage, and insurance schemes can spread the cost of rebuilding. Yet such measures are expensive, and poorer countries and communities usually have the least money to pay for them. This is one reason why international discussions about climate often turn into arguments about fairness, even when the scientific questions are no longer especially disputed.
reading.q: Why can a warmer atmosphere lead to heavier rain?
options: Because warm air makes clouds darker
Because warm air can hold more water
reading.answer: Because warm air can hold more water

reading.passage:
Everyone knows that sleep is important, but until recently scientists had little idea what happens while we are asleep. We now know that the body uses this time to repair itself. The brain also sorts through the day's experiences, keeping what seems useful and letting go of what does not. This is one reason why students who sleep well after studying remember more than those who stay up late.

Sleep happens in cycles of about ninety minutes. In the deepest part of each cycle, the body slows down and breathing becomes regular. In another stage, called REM sleep, the eyes move quickly under closed lids and dreaming is common. Most adults need between seven and nine hours a night, though the exact amount varies from person to person.

Many teenagers go to bed late and get up early for school, so they often sleep less than they need. Experts say that going to bed at the same time every night, and keeping phones out of the bedroom, can make a real difference.
reading.q: According to the passage, what does the brain do during sleep?
options: It sorts through the day's experiences
reading.answer: It sorts through the day's experiences

reading.passage:
Recycling means collecting used materials and turning them into new products. It has become a normal part of life in many countries, and for good reasons. Making new paper from old paper uses less energy than cutting down trees and starting again. Aluminium cans can be melted and reused many times, and a recycled can may be back on a shelf in a few months. Glass, too, can be recycled again and again without losing quality.

However, recycling is not as simple as it looks. Materials must first be sorted, and if a single wrong item is put into a bin, a whole load may be too dirty to sell. Plastic is especially difficult: bottles and food containers are made from different types of plastic, and most of them can only be recycled once or twice.

For this reason, many experts argue that recycling should be the third choice, not the first. The best option is to avoid making waste at all; the next is to reuse what we already have. Recycling remains important, but it cannot solve the problem of waste by itself.
reading.q: Why is plastic difficult to recycle, according to the passage?
options: It is too heavy to collect
Bottles and containers use different types of plastic
reading.answer: Bottles and containers use different types of plastic

reading.passage:
A community garden is a piece of land that local people use to grow vegetables, fruit and flowers. Some gardens are on empty land beside a road. Others are on the roof of a building. People who live nearby can rent a small part of the garden and grow their own food.

These gardens are popular in many cities. They give people a chance to spend time outside and to meet their neighbours. Children can learn where food comes from. Some gardens also give part of their vegetables to food banks, which give free food to people who need it.

A community garden needs hard work. Someone must collect the rent, buy tools and plan the work for the year. In most gardens, the members do this together, and they meet once a month to talk about problems. The meetings are important, because a garden only works when everyone helps.
reading.q: Who can rent a small part of a community garden?
reading.answer: People who live nearby

reading.passage:
Bees do much more than make honey. They also move pollen from one flower to another, and this helps plants make fruit and seeds. Scientists say that a large part of the food we grow depends on the work of bees and other insects.

For a long time, people thought that bees could only be kept in the countryside. Now more and more people keep bees on the roofs of buildings in the city. Bees can find flowers in parks and gardens, and city flowers often have fewer harmful chemicals than farm flowers. City bees may even make more honey than country bees.

Beekeeping is not always easy. A person who wants to keep bees must learn how to look after them, and some people are afraid of bees. For this reason, beekeepers often talk to their neighbours before they put a hive on the roof.

reading.answer: They move pollen between flowers

reading.passage:
Plastic is cheap and strong, and it has changed the way we live. Bags, bottles and food packages are made of it, and most of these things are used only once. When people throw them away, they often end up in rivers and oceans.

Plastic does not rot like food or paper. Sunlight breaks it into very small pieces, but these pieces stay in the water for many years. Fish and sea birds sometimes eat them by mistake, and some animals get caught in larger pieces of plastic. The plastic can also travel long distances, so a bottle dropped in one country may reach a beach in another.

Governments and companies have started to act. Some cities have stopped shops from giving free plastic bags, and some companies now sell drinks in bottles that can be returned and reused. These changes help, but experts say that the most important step is to make less plastic in the first place.

Many people think of a museum as a quiet building full of old objects behind glass. In fact, the best museums are busy places of learning. Visitors can touch copies of ancient tools, listen to stories from people who lived through history, or take part in experiments in a science room. These activities help people understand ideas that a label on a wall can never explain.

Researchers who study how people learn in museums have found something surprising. Visitors usually forget most of the facts they read. They do remember objects that made them feel something, such as a heavy sword, a beautifully painted bowl, or a machine that suddenly worked. Such memories can last for years.

For teachers, this means that a museum visit should not be a race through every room. It is better to spend time on a few objects and to ask questions than to see everything quickly. What students bring home is not a list of dates, but a picture in their minds of how people lived and thought.
reading.q: What can visitors do in the best museums, according to the passage?
options: Touch copies of ancient tools and join activities
Read every label in silence alone
Buy old objects to take home
reading.answer: Touch copies of ancient tools and join activities

Public transport is any system that carries many people at once: buses, trains, trams and underground railways. A single bus can hold more than fifty passengers, which means that one bus can replace dozens of cars on a busy road. For this reason, cities that invest in good public transport often have less traffic and cleaner air.

However, good public transport is expensive. Trains must be built and repaired, and staff must be paid. Fares cover only part of the cost, so the rest must come from taxes. This is why some people ask whether it is fair for everyone to pay for a service that only some people use.

Supporters answer that public transport helps everyone, even those who never travel on it. If buses and trains take cars off the road, drivers save time, and hospitals spend less money on illnesses caused by dirty air. Seen in this way, public transport is not simply a service for passengers; it is an investment in the whole city.
reading.q: What happens in cities that invest in good public transport?
options: There is less traffic and cleaner air
reading.answer: There is less traffic and cleaner air

For most of history, the sky was something people could only look at. That changed in the twentieth century. In 1957, a small satellite called Sputnik became the first human-made object to orbit the Earth, and only twelve years later people walked on the Moon. Since then, spacecraft have visited every planet in our solar system, and telescopes in space have looked back towards the beginning of the universe.

Space travel is extremely expensive, and some people argue that the money would be better spent on problems closer to home, such as health care and clean water. Others point out that space research has given us everyday technologies, from better water filters to satellite navigation. They also argue that studying other planets helps us understand the climate of our own.

Perhaps the strongest argument for space exploration is less practical. Looking at the Earth from far away changes the way people think about it. Many astronauts have described seeing the planet as a small, fragile ball. This experience has led some of them to work for peace and for the protection of the environment.

options: The first human-made satellite began to orbit the Earth
reading.answer: The first human-made satellite began to orbit the Earth

Every new technology changes the kind of work people do, and artificial intelligence is no different. Computers can already write simple reports, answer customers' questions and sort huge amounts of data, work that used to take people many hours. Some jobs will certainly disappear, especially those that involve repeating the same steps again and again.

History suggests, however, that such changes rarely happen as quickly as people fear. When machines took over farm work, millions of people moved into factories; later, when factories became more efficient, many workers found jobs in offices and shops. Each change caused real hardship for some families, but the number of jobs did not simply fall to zero.

The more useful question may be not how many jobs will remain, but which skills will be valued. Tasks that require judgement, creativity and the ability to work with other people are harder for machines to copy. Education systems that teach facts alone may therefore prepare students badly. Those that encourage curiosity, communication and problem-solving are more likely to help young people in a world where the tools they use are changing all the time.
reading.q: According to the passage, which jobs are most likely to disappear?
options: Jobs that involve repeating the same steps
Jobs that involve working with people
reading.answer: Jobs that involve repeating the same steps

Many teenagers go to bed with their phones and wake up with them as well. At first, this seems harmless: a few messages, a video or two, and then sleep. In fact, researchers who study sleep have found that using a phone late at night can make it harder to fall asleep and can make sleep shorter. The light from a screen tells the brain that it is still daytime, and exciting content keeps the mind busy.

There is also a social side to the problem. Messages arrive all night, and young people often feel that they must answer quickly, even when they are tired. This can turn rest into another kind of work. Many teenagers say that they would like to use their phones less at night but do not want to be the first in their group to stop.

Some schools and families are trying simple solutions. They charge phones in the kitchen, set a time after which the phone stays downstairs, or agree that group chats go quiet at night. The aim is not to win a battle against technology, but to protect a few hours in which the mind can rest.
reading.q: What does the light from a screen do, according to researchers?
options: It tells the brain that it is still daytime
It makes the phone battery hot
reading.answer: It tells the brain that it is still daytime

reading.passage:
Anyone who has tried to learn a foreign language knows the strange gap between understanding a rule and being able to use it. A student can explain perfectly when to use the past tense and still say the wrong form in a conversation. Teachers have argued for decades about the reason for this gap and about what should be done in the classroom.

One group believes that grammar should be taught directly, step by step, so that learners build a clear system that they can rely on later. Another group argues that learners acquire language best when they meet many understandable messages, much as children do, and that grammar lessons are of limited value. Many researchers now take a position between these extremes: some focused attention on form helps, but only when it is connected to real use.

What seems beyond doubt is the importance of time and practice. Learners who read and listen widely, and who are not afraid of making mistakes, generally make faster progress than those who wait until they know every rule. In other words, confidence matters as much as knowledge, and it is built by using the language, not by studying it forever.
reading.q: What is the “strange gap” described at the beginning of the passage?
options: The time it takes to learn a language
The difference between knowing a rule and using it correctly
reading.answer: The difference between knowing a rule and using it correctly

reading.passage:
Social media platforms are designed to keep people looking. Their engineers have learned that a new message, a “like” or a short video gives the brain a small reward, and that unclear or upsetting content often holds attention longer than calm and sensible material. The result is a system that is extremely good at what it was built to do, and it is exactly this success that worries critics.

Some of the concern is easy to understand: spending hours online takes time away from sleep, exercise and face-to-face conversation. But a more subtle worry is that the platforms shape what people believe without them noticing. If a person sees mostly posts that agree with their opinions, they may gradually become more certain that everyone thinks as they do, and less willing to consider other views.

Defenders of social media reply that the same tools allow people to organise, learn and find others like themselves. Rather than blaming the technology, they argue that we should teach people to use it deliberately. That means choosing what they follow, noticing when they are being pulled into an argument, and deciding when to put the phone down. Whether individuals can win such a contest against companies that study human attention for a living remains an open question.
reading.q: What holds attention longer, according to the passage?
options: Short messages that are well written
reading.answer: Unclear or upsetting content

reading.passage:
Volunteering is work that people do without being paid, usually to help others or to improve the place where they live. It ranges from serving meals in a shelter to teaching a child to read, from planting trees to running a sports club. To an observer, it can look like a gift: time and effort given freely, with nothing expected in return.

The reality is more complicated, because volunteers usually gain as much as they give. Studies of volunteering repeatedly find that regular volunteers report lower levels of loneliness and greater satisfaction with their lives. Some of this may be self-selection — people who are already cheerful may be more likely to volunteer — but the effect appears in experiments too, especially when the work involves meeting people face to face.

There are difficulties as well. Organisations may rely on volunteers to do work that should really be done by paid staff, and volunteers can feel unsupported or unsure whether their effort matters. The most successful organisations treat volunteers as colleagues rather than as free labour, providing clear tasks, training and honest feedback. The difference between a volunteer who returns for years and one who never comes back is often not enthusiasm. It is how useful they were made to feel on the first day.
reading.q: What do studies of volunteering repeatedly find?
options: Volunteers earn less money than other people
Regular volunteers report lower loneliness and greater satisfaction
Volunteers usually become tired and unhappy
reading.answer: Regular volunteers report lower loneliness and greater satisfaction

reading.passage:
The phrase “extreme weather” covers events such as heatwaves, heavy rainfall, droughts and very powerful storms. Such events have always existed, but a growing body of research suggests that a warmer atmosphere changes both their frequency and their strength. Warm air can hold more water, so when rain finally falls it may fall harder; hotter and drier seasons, meanwhile, leave forests and farmland ready to burn.

Attributing any single storm to climate change is difficult, and scientists are usually careful to say that a particular event “was made more likely” rather than that it “was caused” by warming. Nevertheless, statistical work that compares thousands of simulations with and without human influence has become increasingly confident. For some heatwaves, researchers now describe the effect as unmistakable.

The practical question is how cities and farmers should respond. Dams, early-warning systems and trees that shade streets can all reduce damage, and insurance schemes can spread the cost of rebuilding. Yet such measures are expensive, and poorer countries and communities usually have the least money to pay for them. This is one reason why international discussions about climate often turn into arguments about fairness, even when the scientific questions are no longer especially disputed.
reading.q: Why can a warmer atmosphere lead to heavier rain?
options: Because warm air makes clouds darker
Because warm air can hold more water
reading.answer: Because warm air can hold more water

reading.passage:
Remote work means doing paid work outside a company's office, usually from home and usually with the help of the internet. Although the idea is not new, it became far more common during the COVID-19 pandemic, when millions of employees were asked to stay at home. Many of them found that they saved time and money on travelling, and some employers discovered that they could reduce the cost of their offices.

Yet the shift has not been entirely positive. Employees who live alone sometimes report feeling isolated, while others find it difficult to stop working in the evening, because the line between home and office has disappeared. Managers, meanwhile, worry that new members of staff learn less quickly when they cannot listen to more experienced colleagues.

Most companies have therefore settled on a mixed arrangement, with staff working in the office for part of the week and at home for the rest. Supporters of this approach argue that it keeps the flexibility of remote work while protecting the informal contact that helps teams solve problems together. Critics, however, point out that such arrangements often benefit office workers far more than people who work in shops, hospitals or factories.
reading.q: What did some employers discover during the pandemic?
reading.answer: They could reduce office costs

reading.passage:
For most of the last century, the world's economy worked in a straight line. Companies took raw materials, made products, and sold them. When the products broke or went out of fashion, they were thrown away. This is often called the “take-make-dispose” model, and it assumes that resources are unlimited.

The circular economy offers a different picture. In a circular system, materials are kept in use for as long as possible. Products are designed so that they can be repaired, shared or taken apart, and when they finally fail, their parts become raw materials for something else. Supporters claim that this approach could cut waste dramatically and reduce the demand for new resources. In some industries the idea is already working: several car makers now remanufacture engines, and some clothing companies collect old garments to make new fibres.

Yet the circular economy has critics too. They argue that efficiency gains can be cancelled out by what economists call the rebound effect: when products become cheaper to make, people simply buy more of them, so total consumption may not fall at all. Others point out that recycling a material is rarely lossless. For these reasons, even enthusiastic supporters admit that circular design must be combined with limits on how much we consume.
reading.q: According to the passage, what happens to products in a circular system when they finally fail?
options: They are thrown away like other waste
Their parts become raw materials for something else
They are sold at a lower price
reading.answer: Their parts become raw materials for something else

The roots take in water and minerals from the soil, and they also hold the plant in the ground. When the plant is fully grown, it makes flowers. reading.passage:
A community garden is a piece of land that local people use to grow vegetables, fruit and flowers. Some gardens are on empty land beside a road. Others are on the roof of a building. People who live nearby can rent a small part of the garden and grow their own food.

These gardens are popular in many cities. They give people a chance to spend time outside and to meet their neighbours. Children can learn where food comes from. Some gardens also give part of their vegetables to food banks, which give free food to people who need it.

A community garden needs hard work. Someone must collect the rent, buy tools and plan the work for the year. In most gardens, the members do this together, and they meet once a month to talk about problems. The meetings are important, because a garden only works when everyone helps.
reading.q: Who can rent a small part of a community garden?
reading.answer: People who live nearby

reading.passage:
Bees do much more than make honey. They also move pollen from one flower to another, and this helps plants make fruit and seeds. Scientists say that a large part of the food we grow depends on the work of bees and other insects.

For a long time, people thought that bees could only be kept in the countryside. Now more and more people keep bees on the roofs of buildings in the city. Bees can find flowers in parks and gardens, and city flowers often have fewer harmful chemicals than farm flowers. City bees may even make more honey than country bees.

Beekeeping is not always easy. A person who wants to keep bees must learn how to look after them, and some people are afraid of bees. For this reason, beekeepers often talk to their neighbours before they put a hive on the roof.

reading.answer: They move pollen between flowers

Many people think of a museum as a quiet building full of old objects behind glass. In fact, the best museums are busy places of learning. Visitors can touch copies of ancient tools, listen to stories from people who lived through history, or take part in experiments in a science room. These activities help people understand ideas that a label on a wall can never explain.

Researchers who study how people learn in museums have found something surprising. Visitors usually forget most of the facts they read. They do remember objects that made them feel something, such as a heavy sword, a beautifully painted bowl, or a machine that suddenly worked. Such memories can last for years.

For teachers, this means that a museum visit should not be a race through every room. It is better to spend time on a few objects and to ask questions than to see everything quickly. What students bring home is not a list of dates, but a picture in their minds of how people lived and thought.

options: Touch copies of ancient tools and join activities
Read every label in silence alone
Buy old objects to take home
reading.answer: Touch copies of ancient tools and join activities

Public transport is any system that carries many people at once: buses, trains, trams and underground railways. A single bus can hold more than fifty passengers, which means that one bus can replace dozens of cars on a busy road. For this reason, cities that invest in good public transport often have less traffic and cleaner air.

However, good public transport is expensive. Trains must be built and repaired, and staff must be paid. Fares cover only part of the cost, so the rest must come from taxes. This is why some people ask whether it is fair for everyone to pay for a service that only some people use.

Supporters answer that public transport helps everyone, even those who never travel on it. If buses and trains take cars off the road, drivers save time, and hospitals spend less money on illnesses caused by dirty air. Seen in this way, public transport is not simply a service for passengers; it is an investment in the whole city.
reading.q: What happens in cities that invest in good public transport?
options: There is less traffic and cleaner air
reading.answer: There is less traffic and cleaner air

For most of history, the sky was something people could only look at. That changed in the twentieth century. In 1957, a small satellite called Sputnik became the first human-made object to orbit the Earth, and only twelve years later people walked on the Moon. Since then, spacecraft have visited every planet in our solar system, and telescopes in space have looked back towards the beginning of the universe.

Space travel is extremely expensive, and some people argue that the money would be better spent on problems closer to home, such as health care and clean water. Others point out that space research has given us everyday technologies, from better water filters to satellite navigation. They also argue that studying other planets helps us understand the climate of our own.

Perhaps the strongest argument for space exploration is less practical. Looking at the Earth from far away changes the way people think about it. Many astronauts have described seeing the planet as a small, fragile ball. This experience has led some of them to work for peace and for the protection of the environment.
reading.q: What happened in 1957?
options: The first human-made satellite began to orbit the Earth
reading.answer: The first human-made satellite began to orbit the Earth

reading.passage:
Every new technology changes the kind of work people do, and artificial intelligence is no different. Computers can already write simple reports, answer customers' questions and sort huge amounts of data, work that used to take people many hours. Some jobs will certainly disappear, especially those that involve repeating the same steps again and again.

History suggests, however, that such changes rarely happen as quickly as people fear. When machines took over farm work, millions of people moved into factories; later, when factories became more efficient, many workers found jobs in offices and shops. Each change caused real hardship for some families, but the number of jobs did not simply fall to zero.

The more useful question may be not how many jobs will remain, but which skills will be valued. Tasks that require judgement, creativity and the ability to work with other people are harder for machines to copy. Education systems that teach facts alone may therefore prepare students badly. Those that encourage curiosity, communication and problem-solving are more likely to help young people in a world where the tools they use are changing all the time.
reading.q: According to the passage, which jobs are most likely to disappear?
options: Jobs that involve repeating the same steps
Jobs that involve working with people
reading.answer: Jobs that involve repeating the same steps

Many teenagers go to bed with their phones and wake up with them as well. At first, this seems harmless: a few messages, a video or two, and then sleep. In fact, researchers who study sleep have found that using a phone late at night can make it harder to fall asleep and can make sleep shorter. The light from a screen tells the brain that it is still daytime, and exciting content keeps the mind busy.

There is also a social side to the problem. Messages arrive all night, and young people often feel that they must answer quickly, even when they are tired. This can turn rest into another kind of work. Many teenagers say that they would like to use their phones less at night but do not want to be the first in their group to stop.

Some schools and families are trying simple solutions. They charge phones in the kitchen, set a time after which the phone stays downstairs, or agree that group chats go quiet at night. The aim is not to win a battle against technology, but to protect a few hours in which the mind can rest.
reading.q: What does the light from a screen do, according to researchers?
options: It tells the brain that it is still daytime
It makes the phone battery hot
reading.answer: It tells the brain that it is still daytime

reading.passage:
Anyone who has tried to learn a foreign language knows the strange gap between understanding a rule and being able to use it. A student can explain perfectly when to use the past tense and still say the wrong form in a conversation. Teachers have argued for decades about the reason for this gap and about what should be done in the classroom.

One group believes that grammar should be taught directly, step by step, so that learners build a clear system that they can rely on later. Another group argues that learners acquire language best when they meet many understandable messages, much as children do, and that grammar lessons are of limited value. Many researchers now take a position between these extremes: some focused attention on form helps, but only when it is connected to real use.

What seems beyond doubt is the importance of time and practice. Learners who read and listen widely, and who are not afraid of making mistakes, generally make faster progress than those who wait until they know every rule. In other words, confidence matters as much as knowledge, and it is built by using the language, not by studying it forever.
reading.q: What is the “strange gap” described at the beginning of the passage?
options: The time it takes to learn a language
The difference between knowing a rule and using it correctly
reading.answer: The difference between knowing a rule and using it correctly

Social media platforms are designed to keep people looking. Their engineers have learned that a new message, a “like” or a short video gives the brain a small reward, and that unclear or upsetting content often holds attention longer than calm and sensible material. The result is a system that is extremely good at what it was built to do, and it is exactly this success that worries critics.

Some of the concern is easy to understand: spending hours online takes time away from sleep, exercise and face-to-face conversation. But a more subtle worry is that the platforms shape what people believe without them noticing. If a person sees mostly posts that agree with their opinions, they may gradually become more certain that everyone thinks as they do, and less willing to consider other views.

Defenders of social media reply that the same tools allow people to organise, learn and find others like themselves. Social media platforms are designed to keep people looking. Their engineers have learned that a new message, a “like” or a short video gives the brain a small reward, and that unclear or upsetting content often holds attention longer than calm and sensible material. reading.passage:
Volunteering is work that people do without being paid, usually to help others or to improve the place where they live. It ranges from serving meals in a shelter to teaching a child to read, from planting trees to running a sports club. To an observer, it can look like a gift: time and effort given freely, with nothing expected in return.

The reality is more complicated, because volunteers usually gain as much as they give. Studies of volunteering repeatedly find that regular volunteers report lower levels of loneliness and greater satisfaction with their lives. Some of this may be self-selection — people who are already cheerful may be more likely to volunteer — but the effect appears in experiments too, especially when the work involves meeting people face to face.

There are difficulties as well. Organisations may rely on volunteers to do work that should really be done by paid staff, and volunteers can feel unsupported or unsure whether their effort matters. The most successful organisations treat volunteers as colleagues rather than as free labour, providing clear tasks, training and honest feedback. The difference between a volunteer who returns for years and one who never comes back is often not enthusiasm. It is how useful they were made to feel on the first day.
reading.q: What do studies of volunteering repeatedly find?
options: Volunteers earn less money than other people
Regular volunteers report lower loneliness and greater satisfaction
Volunteers usually become tired and unhappy
reading.answer: Regular volunteers report lower loneliness and greater satisfaction

reading.passage:
The phrase “extreme weather” covers events such as heatwaves, heavy rainfall, droughts and very powerful storms. Such events have always existed, but a growing body of research suggests that a warmer atmosphere changes both their frequency and their strength. Warm air can hold more water, so when rain finally falls it may fall harder; hotter and drier seasons, meanwhile, leave forests and farmland ready to burn.

Attributing any single storm to climate change is difficult, and scientists are usually careful to say that a particular event “was made more likely” rather than that it “was caused” by warming. Nevertheless, statistical work that compares thousands of simulations with and without human influence has become increasingly confident. For some heatwaves, researchers now describe the effect as unmistakable.

The practical question is how cities and farmers should respond. Dams, early-warning systems and trees that shade streets can all reduce damage, and insurance schemes can spread the cost of rebuilding. Yet such measures are expensive, and poorer countries and communities usually have the least money to pay for them. This is one reason why international discussions about climate often turn into arguments about fairness, even when the scientific questions are no longer especially disputed.
reading.q: Why can a warmer atmosphere lead to heavier rain?
options: Because warm air makes clouds darker
Because warm air can hold more water
reading.answer: Because warm air can hold more water

reading.passage:
Remote work means doing paid work outside a company's office, usually from home and usually with the help of the internet. Although the idea is not new, it became far more common during the COVID-19 pandemic, when millions of employees were asked to stay at home. Many of them found that they saved time and money on travelling, and some employers discovered that they could reduce the cost of their offices.

Yet the shift has not been entirely positive. Employees who live alone sometimes report feeling isolated, while others find it difficult to stop working in the evening, because the line between home and office has disappeared. Managers, meanwhile, worry that new members of staff learn less quickly when they cannot listen to more experienced colleagues.

Most companies have therefore settled on a mixed arrangement, with staff working in the office for part of the week and at home for the rest. Supporters of this approach argue that it keeps the flexibility of remote work while protecting the informal contact that helps teams solve problems together. Critics, however, point out that such arrangements often benefit office workers far more than people who work in shops, hospitals or factories.
reading.q: What did some employers discover during the pandemic?
reading.answer: They could reduce office costs

reading.passage:
For most of the last century, the world's economy worked in a straight line. Companies took raw materials, made products, and sold them. When the products broke or went out of fashion, they were thrown away. This is often called the “take-make-dispose” model, and it assumes that resources are unlimited.

The circular economy offers a different picture. In a circular system, materials are kept in use for as long as possible. Products are designed so that they can be repaired, shared or taken apart, and when they finally fail, their parts become raw materials for something else. Supporters claim that this approach could cut waste dramatically and reduce the demand for new resources. In some industries the idea is already working: several car makers now remanufacture engines, and some clothing companies collect old garments to make new fibres.

Yet the circular economy has critics too. They argue that efficiency gains can be cancelled out by what economists call the rebound effect: when products become cheaper to make, people simply buy more of them, so total consumption may not fall at all. Others point out that recycling a material is rarely lossless. For these reasons, even enthusiastic supporters admit that circular design must be combined with limits on how much we consume.
reading.q: According to the passage, what happens to products in a circular system when they finally fail?
options: They are thrown away like other waste
Their parts become raw materials for something else
They are sold at a lower price
reading.answer: Their parts become raw materials for something else

reading.passage:
A community garden is a piece of land that local people use to grow vegetables, fruit and flowers. Some gardens are on empty land beside a road. Others are on the roof of a building. People who live nearby can rent a small part of the garden and grow their own food.

These gardens are popular in many cities. They give people a chance to spend time outside and to meet their neighbours. Children can learn where food comes from. Some gardens also give part of their vegetables to food banks, which give free food to people who need it.

A community garden needs hard work. Someone must collect the rent, buy tools and plan the work for the year. In most gardens, the members do this together, and they meet once a month to talk about problems. The meetings are important, because a garden only works when everyone helps.
reading.q: Who can rent a small part of a community garden?
reading.answer: People who live nearby

Bees do much more than make honey. They also move pollen from one flower to another, and this helps plants make fruit and seeds. Scientists say that a large part of the food we grow depends on the work of bees and other insects.

For a long time, people thought that bees could only be kept in the countryside. Now more and more people keep bees on the roofs of buildings in the city. Bees can find flowers in parks and gardens, and city flowers often have fewer harmful chemicals than farm flowers. City bees may even make more honey than country bees.

Beekeeping is not always easy. A person who wants to keep bees must learn how to look after them, and some people are afraid of bees. For this reason, beekeepers often talk to their neighbours before they put a hive on the roof.

Plastic is cheap and strong, and it has changed the way we live. Bags, bottles and food packages are made of it, and most of these things are used only once. When people throw them away, they often end up in rivers and oceans.

Plastic does not rot like food or paper. Sunlight breaks it into very small pieces, but these pieces stay in the water for many years. Fish and sea birds sometimes eat them by mistake, and some animals get caught in larger pieces of plastic. The plastic can also travel long distances, so a bottle dropped in one country may reach a beach in another.

Governments and companies have started to act. Some cities have stopped shops from giving free plastic bags, and some companies now sell drinks in bottles that can be returned and reused. These changes help, but experts say that the most important step is to make less plastic in the first place.

reading.answer: It breaks into very small pieces
